sbh2.0:1.0: Yogasthāna II opens by naming the *two paths* of dispassion — the worldly (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*) — and their shared requisite-stage, *naiṣkramyabhūmi* (treated in detail at [sbh1.3](sbh1.3.html)). The whole of YS II proceeds on this two-path framework: from the analytic question 'who [are the practitioners]?' (paragraphs 2–19) through 'what [do they practice on]?' (paragraphs 30+) up to the actual yogic operations of [sbh2.1](sbh2.1.html) onward. Paragraph 1 is therefore the architectural hinge of the whole second yogasthāna.
sbh2.0:2.1: The seventeen-question framework at 2.1–2.17 is the table of contents for all of Yogasthāna II. Each question is answered at length in turn: persons (paragraphs 2–19), delineation (20–36), object (paragraphs handed off to [sbh2.1](sbh2.1.html)–[sbh2.7](sbh2.7.html)), instruction (47–48), training (49–55), dharmas conducive to training (56–64), loss-of-yoga and yogas (the *yoga* chapters), mental engagement, and so on. The same seventeen-fold structure recurs (with variant ordering) in the corresponding sections of *Bodhisattvabhūmi*; the parallel marks this as canonical Yogācāra scholastic procedure rather than text-specific structure.
sbh2.0:2.20: The twenty-eight person-types fall into four functional groups: (1) *faculty-typing* (1–2: mild/sharp), (2) *defilement-typing* (3–9: lust-, hatred-, delusion-, conceit-, vitarka-intoxicated; balanced; slight-dust), (3) *path-stage-typing* (10–19: practitioner, fruit-attainer, faith-/dharma-follower, śraddhādhimukta, dṛṣṭiprāpta, kāyasākṣin, one-birth-at-most, family-to-family, one-interval, three antarāparinirvāyin, upapadya-parinirvāyin, the with/without-effort pair, upstream-goer), (4) *liberation-typing* (samaya-vimukta, akopya-dharman, prajñā-vimukta, ubhayatobhāga-vimukta). The same twenty-eight-fold list appears in the Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* with minor renumbering — the typology is canonical to the path-fruit literature, not a Yogācāra innovation. Apparatus notes: *samaprāpta* is rendered as the balanced person and distinguished from *samabhāgacarita* (even-balanced conduct) at 23.7; *mandarajaska* is kept in brackets rather than normalized to *alparajaska*. The printed list at 2.32 has *buddhādhimukta*, but the definition at 10.3–10.8 requires *śraddhādhimukta*; the printed list at 2.39 gives only *sābhisaṁskāra-parinirvāyin*, but the twenty-eight count and the definition at 15.1–15.2 require the paired *anabhisaṁskāra-parinirvāyin*; and the printed list at 2.42 has *prajñādhimuktaḥ*, but the definition at 19.1–19.4 requires *prajñā-vimukta*. The English follows the defined categories while leaving the Sanskrit root unchanged.
sbh2.0:2.48: *Indriya-prabheda* — the cross-reference is to the gotrabhūmi treatment of mild/middle/sharp faculty at [sbh1.1:13](sbh1.1.html#sbh1.1:13.1). The text inherits the prior definition rather than re-defining; the *as before* shorthand is the same convention used at [sbh1.3:2.5](sbh1.3.html#sbh1.3:2.5) for the saṁbhāra-cluster. The *dhandha-/manda-vāhin* pair is rendered functionally as slow-functioning / weak-functioning rather than the mechanical 'slowly/weakly borne.'
sbh2.0:13.2: The *triṇi-saṁyojanāni* (three fetters) — *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (personality-view), *śīlavrata-parāmarśa* (clinging-to-virtue-and-vow), and *vicikitsā* (doubt) — are the canonical defilements abandoned at stream-entry (*srotaāpatti*). Standard list across Sarvāstivāda, Yogācāra, and Theravāda. Their abandonment marks the *darśana-mārga* — the practitioner has *seen* the truths and is no longer fundamentally at risk of falling back.
sbh2.0:14.5: The three sparks-of-fire similes (14.6, 14.10, 14.14–15) for the three *antarā-parinirvāyin* sub-types are canonical: (1) a spark that goes out at once = nirvāṇa at the moment of intermediate-existence generation; (2) a spark from a hammered iron-pot that flies and dies in mid-air = nirvāṇa some time into the antarābhava; (3) a spark that almost reaches the ground = nirvāṇa just before re-birth. The same simile-triad appears in the Pāli Anguttara and in Sarvāstivāda Vibhāṣā literature; preserved here because the three-fold subdivision of antarā-parinirvāyin is doctrinally significant.
sbh2.0:11.6: The printed/root repeats *parato-'vavāda-anuśāsanī-mārga* ('path of admonition-and-instruction from another') from the faith-resolved definition, but that contradicts the immediately preceding dharma-follower definition at 9.2–10.2. Since *dṛṣṭiprāpta* is the fruit-attainer corresponding to *dharmānusārin*, English restores the expected negative sense and marks the line conjectural/corrupt.
sbh2.0:16.4: *Cyavitvā* in the upstream-goer definition means 'having passed away' from the first dhyāna rebirth, not doctrinal falling-back. The non-returner ascends by successive rebirths to Akaniṣṭha or the neither-perception-nor-non-perception sphere.
sbh2.0:17.4: *samaya-vimukta* — 'sometimes-liberated,' i.e., one whose liberation is conditional on continued effort and is at risk of falling back. The mild-faculty arhat. Paragraphs 17.4–17.10 describe the three causes of vulnerability: falling back from pleasure-dwellings, considering self-death (to safeguard liberation), and protective vigilance under fear of heedlessness. The opposite — *akopya-dharman* (paragraph 18) — is the sharp-faculty arhat whose liberation is unshakable. The sixfold arhat-typology (samaya-vimukta + five akopya types) is Sarvāstivāda canonical; the present text preserves it but treats it briefly because the typology is presupposed in the rest of YS II.
sbh2.0:20.3: The eleven divisions for delineating persons — by faculty, community (*nikāya*), conduct (*carita*), vow (*praṇidhāna*), practice (*pratipatti*), path-fruit (*mārga-phala*), application (*prayoga*), attainment (*samāpatti*), rebirth (*upapatti*), falling-back (*parihāṇi*), and obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) — comprise the analytic grid by which any practitioner can be classified. Here *nikāya* means the sevenfold Buddhist community classification (monk, nun, probationer, novices, layman, laywoman), not sectarian school. The original enumeration at 20.3 dropped 'by division of practice'; restored in brackets, since paragraphs 30–31 actually unfold that division (the four *pratipad* matrix of painful/pleasant × slow/quick-knowledge).
sbh2.0:25.14: *Eḍamūka* and *hastasaṁbādhika* occur in incapacity lists at 25.14 and 88.42. The English now reads 'deaf-mute' and 'hand-impaired' rather than the slash hedge 'hand-tied [/maimed]' or the doubled 'mute, dumb.' The point is incapacity affecting communication/manual function, not a specific punishment image.
sbh2.0:30.6: The fourfold *pratipad* classification — *duḥkhā/sukhā pratipad* × *dhandha-/kṣipra-abhijñā* (painful/pleasant practice × slow/quick knowledge) — is canonical across Sarvāstivāda, Theravāda, and Yogācāra. The intended Yogācāra matrix at 31.1–4 ties it specifically to attainment level (preliminary dhyāna *anāgamya* vs. full basic dhyāna *maula-dhyāna*) crossed with faculty (mild vs. sharp). The printed/root Sanskrit at 31.1–31.2 reads *maula-dhyāna-lābhin* for the painful-practice pair as well, collapsing the painful/pleasant contrast; the English treats this as a source corruption and restores *anāgamya* for the two painful-practice cases. 'Painful' here does not mean physical pain but the difficulty of progress when concentration is incomplete; 'pleasant' means progress carried by the easeful joy of the basic dhyāna.
sbh2.0:33.9: The eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) at 33.9–12 are the canonical list: (1) one with form sees forms, (2) inwardly without perception of form sees external forms, (3) realizes the pure-liberation with the body, (4–7) the four formless attainments, (8) the cessation of perception-and-feeling. The body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) is defined precisely as the one who attains these eight in forward and reverse order without yet attaining arhatship — distinct from the both-ways-liberated arhat (34.6–8) who attains *both* the eight vimokṣas *and* the destruction of fluxes.
sbh2.0:33.4: The printed/root `parapratyaya-vinayānusāreṇa` makes the dharma-follower follow a discipline dependent on another's condition, contradicting the definition at 9.2–10.2 where he is self-capable and does not seek admonition-and-instruction from another. The English restores the expected negative sense, effectively reading `a-parapratyaya-`, and marks the line as conjectural.
sbh2.0:34.5: The two obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) at 34.5 — *kleśa-āvaraṇa* (defilement-obscuration) and *samāpatti-āvaraṇa* (attainment-obscuration) — divide the arhats into wisdom-liberated (clears only the first) and both-ways-liberated (clears both). The *samāpatti-āvaraṇa* is specifically the inability to enter the eight vimokṣa attainments at will — not a moral defilement but a residual incapacity of the meditative substrate. Distinct from the *jñeya-āvaraṇa* (knowable-obscuration) discussed in later Yogācāra; that is a Mahāyāna concern, not relevant to the present Śrāvakabhūmi typology.
sbh2.0:35.6: The two kinds of grossness (*audārika*) — *svabhāva* (in essential nature) and *saṁkhyā* (in number/quantity) — formalize the worldly-path comparison technique. The practitioner ascending through the eight samāpattis sees the lower stage as both *qualitatively* more flawed (more painful, less durable) and *quantitatively* more extensive in its aggregates-to-be-abandoned. This pair-analysis is preserved exactly into the later *vairāgya* technical literature.
sbh2.0:36.12: The pivotal contrast: the worldly path uses the *grossness-versus-peace* object, the supramundane path uses the *four noble truths* object (36.17–18). This is the architectural distinction between *laukika-vairāgya* and *lokottara-vairāgya* introduced at [sbh1.3:1](sbh1.3.html#sbh1.3:1.1). The worldly path abandons defilements stage-by-stage but not absolutely (they re-arise); the supramundane path uproots them through the four truths.
sbh2.0:40.14: *Svalakṣaṇa* is rendered as 'specific characteristic,' matching the vipaśyanā and skill-object chapters. Earlier 'own-mark' was a literal calque but made the same technical category look terminologically separate.
sbh2.0:41.6: The threefold suffering schema — *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (suffering-of-suffering, i.e., painful feeling itself), *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (suffering of change, i.e., the instability of pleasant feeling and the suffering that arises in defilements as they shift), and *saṁskāra-duḥkhatā* (suffering of conditioning, i.e., the all-pervasive insecurity of the conditioned aggregates themselves) — is canonical Sarvāstivāda-Yogācāra abhidharma. The first is recognized by everyone; the second and third require Dharma-instruction. The chapter's compact analysis at 41.4–46.5 is the standard expansion of the brief sūtra-formula at 37.2–3.
sbh2.0:42.4: *Apriya-vinābhāva* is 'separation from the unloved,' the positive counterpart to *priya-vinābhāva* ('separation from the loved') in the suffering formula. The previous 'non-separation from the loved' duplicated the already listed union-with-the-loved counterpart and lost the full opposite-pair structure.
sbh2.0:44.1: The printed/root *mātṛgrāmasya hastigrahaṇaṁ* is likely corrupt for *hasta-grahaṇa* ('taking a woman by the hand'), a stock sensual-contact example. Reading *hasti* literally as 'elephant' makes no sense in the suffering-of-change proof. English marks the repair conjectural/corrupt.
sbh2.0:46.19: The four *ālambana* (objects) named here — *vyāpī*, *carita-viśodhana*, *kauśalya*, *kleśa-viśodhana* — are the architectural map of the entire object-discussion in YS II–III: *vyāpī* gets [sbh2.1](sbh2.1.html), *carita-viśodhana* gets [sbh2.2](sbh2.2.html)–[sbh2.6](sbh2.6.html) (the five carita-matched practices), *kauśalya* gets [sbh2.7](sbh2.7.html), and *kleśa-viśodhana* is the worldly path's grossness/calmness pair already treated at 35.1–36.16 above. The four-fold typology is repeated verbatim at [sbh2.1:1.5](sbh2.1.html#sbh2.1:1.5).
sbh2.0:48.2: The printed/root *dharmasattvaṁ* in the definition of unperverted instruction is awkward but points to Dharma plus what is real/true, not to an abstract 'meaning of being.' It may reflect *dharma-tattva* or a close real/truth expression; the English keeps the low-risk sense 'Dharma and reality' rather than adding a slash hedge.
sbh2.0:48.28: The three *prātihārya* (wonders) — psychic power (*ṛddhi*), mind-reading (*ādeśanā*), and admonition (*anuśāsanī*) — are the canonical list from the Pāli Kevaddha-sutta (DN 11) and parallel Sanskrit sources. The Yogācāra reading at 48.31–37 treats them as a pedagogical sequence: psychic display gains the hearer's respect, mind-reading lets the teacher diagnose the hearer's faculties, admonition delivers the appropriate antidote.
sbh2.0:49.4: The *triśikṣā* (three trainings) — *adhiśīla, adhicitta, adhiprajñā* (higher virtue, higher mind, higher wisdom) — is canonical across all Buddhist traditions. The Yogācāra analysis at 53.17–26 distinguishes two senses of *adhi-*: (1) pre-eminence (each training is supreme of its kind), and (2) higher referent (each takes the next-higher training as its object/aim). This dual analysis is preserved exactly in the text.
sbh2.0:55.17: The three *vimokṣa-mukha* (doors of liberation) — emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), signlessness (*animitta*) — is canonical. The Yogācāra mapping at 55.21–30 ties each to a specific object-relation: wishlessness arises from seeing fault in the conditioned (no wish toward it); signlessness arises from seeing nirvāṇa as the way out (signless because nirvāṇa is unconditioned); emptiness arises from seeing the unreality of self/being/soul/person. The triadic structure echoes the *three lakṣaṇa* (impermanence, suffering, non-self) in different idiom.
sbh2.0:56.30: The line introduces ten perceptions but the printed/root list yields only nine unless bare *anitya-saṁjñā* is supplied before *anitye duḥkha-saṁjñā*. The supplement also restores the standard progression impermanence -> suffering-in-the-impermanent -> non-self-in-suffering. Sanskrit JSON is left unchanged; the English marks the supplied perception as conjectural. *Āhāre pratikūla-saṁjñā* is rendered 'perception of food as repugnant,' following the glossary distinction between *pratikūla* (repugnant/averse) and *aśubha* (unattractive/impure/repulsive by context).
sbh2.0:59.126: The four *manaskāra* (mental engagements) — *bala-vāhana* (forceful), *sacchidra-vāhana* (interrupted), *niścchidra-vāhana* (uninterrupted), *anābhoga-vāhana* (effortless) — are paired one-to-one with the nine stages of mental abiding at [sbh3.1:13–14](sbh3.1.html#sbh3.1:13.1). This is one of the most important architectural mappings in the Śrāvakabhūmi: the four-mode progression names *how* the practitioner sustains attention across the nine stages of stabilization. The English drops a mechanical '-borne' calque for readability while preserving the Sanskrit labels in brackets.
sbh2.0:60.11: The four *nimitta* (signs) — object-sign (*ālambana-nimitta*), cause-sign (*nidāna-nimitta*), sign-to-be-avoided (*parivarjanīya-nimitta*), and sign-to-be-resorted-to (*niṣevaṇīya-nimitta*) — are the local Yogācāra typology of what the meditator engages with. The original enumeration at 60.12–14 dropped 'cause-sign' (treated separately at 61.1+); restored in brackets.
sbh2.0:62.8: The nine kinds of *adhimokṣa* (resolve) at 62.9–13 are an unusual nine-fold list rather than the more familiar three-fold or four-fold; the analysis at 63.1–64.11 unpacks them as parameter-pairs (luminous/not-luminous, dull/sharp, limited/great, limited/boundless, pure/not-pure). The 'resolve' here is the mental act by which the practitioner takes hold of a meditation-object on the concentrated plane. At 63.3 the printed/root Sanskrit repeats *sūdgṛhīte* ('well grasped') for the not-luminous case, but the contrast with 63.1 requires 'not well grasped'; the English restores the negative and marks the line conjectural.
sbh2.0:64.17: *āśraya-nirodha* and *āśraya-parivṛtti* — the two transformations of the *āśraya* (basis/substrate). *āśraya-parivṛtti* is one of the most important Yogācāra technical terms: the deep structural change in the practitioner's psychophysical basis that occurs when meditative practice fully matures. Not a state-attainment but a change in the substrate that produces states. The pair here connects directly to the *kārya-pariniṣpatti* (consummation of the work) treatment at [sbh2.1:8.5+](sbh2.1.html#sbh2.1:8.5).
sbh2.0:65.3: The three *yogācāra* types — *ādikarmika* (beginner), *kṛta-paricaya* (experienced), *atikrānta-manaskāra* (one who has gone beyond mental engagement) — are paired one-to-one with the seven attentions (*sapta-manaskāra*) treated in detail at [sbh4.1](sbh4.1.html). The text gives two parallel definitions of the three (67.1–14 and 67.15–26): the first by relation to the seven attentions (beginner = pre-attainment of *lakṣaṇa-pratisaṁvedī*; experienced = working through the remaining six attentions; gone-beyond = arrived at the fruit-of-completion-of-practice attention); the second by relation to the *nirvedha-bhāgīya* (penetration-conducive wholesome roots: warmth, summits, patience, supreme worldly dharmas). The two definitions converge at arhatship.
sbh2.0:67.19: The four *nirvedha-bhāgīya* (penetration-conducive wholesome roots) — *uṣmagata* (warmth), *mūrdhan* (summits), *satya-anulomikī kṣānti* (truth-conforming patience), and *laukikāgra-dharma* (supreme worldly dharmas) — mark the immediate pre-darśanamārga stage. Canonical in Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* (VI.18–24) and Yogācāra alike. At 67.20-67.21 the root splits *satyānulomāḥ* from *kṣāntayaḥ* across segment boundaries; the English keeps them together as the single technical item. The disciple traverses these four in sequence at the close of the *prayoga-mārga* before descending into the *niyāma* (the fixedness of the noble lineage, sometimes called the *samyaktva-niyāma*) — at which moment the *darśana-mārga* commences.
sbh2.0:67.90: The thirty-seven awakening-side factors are compressed and noisy at 67.78–92. The bases of psychic power should be read as the standard four — desire-, energy-, mind-, and investigation-concentration, each endowed with formative impulses for abandonment. The printed/root powers list at 67.90 omits *vīrya* even though the five powers must parallel the five faculties; the English supplies energy conjecturally and marks the repair.
sbh2.0:68.4: The four *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) — body, feeling, mind, and dharmas — structure the entirety of ¶¶68–77. The chapter analyzes each object in turn (body at 68–69, feeling at 72–74, mind at 75, dharmas at 75.39+), then unpacks the contemplation under three rubrics: *ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna* (object-foundation), *svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna* (own-nature foundation: the mindfulness-and-wisdom that uphold concentration), and *saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna* (conjunction-foundation: associated mental-factor dharmas), at 77.60–64. The pairing with the four *viparyāsa* (perversions) at 77.8–28 — body/pure-in-unclean, feeling/pleasant-in-painful, mind/permanent-in-impermanent, dharmas/self-in-not-self — is the canonical functional analysis (preserved verbatim in Pāli at SN 47 and in *Abhidharmakośa* VI.14–17).
sbh2.0:69.7: The text says contemplation (*anupaśyanā*) is threefold at 69.6 but the printed/root line at 69.7 gives only hearing-born and cultivation-born wisdom. The later summary at 77.68 explicitly gives the normal triad — hearing-born, reflection-born, and cultivation-born — so the English supplies *cintā-mayī prajñā* conjecturally.
sbh2.0:73.2: The printed/root mind-list omits *vigata-rāgaṁ cittaṁ* in the opening enumeration, but the line claims twenty minds and the definition at 75.1–75.3 explicitly defines both mind-with-lust and mind-without-lust. The English supplies the missing second half of the pair and marks it conjectural.
sbh2.0:71.14: The four *ālambana* (objects) named here for the foundations of mindfulness — *vyāpī, carita-viśodhana, kauśalya, kleśa-viśodhana* — are the same four-fold scheme treated structurally at [sbh2.0:46.19](sbh2.0.html#sbh2.0:46.19) and unfolded across [sbh2.1](sbh2.1.html)–[sbh2.7](sbh2.7.html). Their reappearance at 71.13–14 ties the *smṛtyupasthāna* framework directly into the chapter's overarching object-architecture: mindfulness 'binds' to one of these four kinds of object, and the foundation it establishes is named by reference to that object.
sbh2.0:72.8: The feeling taxonomy uses *sāmiṣa/nirāmiṣa* and *gardhāśrita/naiṣkramyāśrita*. The prior bracket *gṛhāśrita* imported a householder-dependent category not present in this root; 74.3 defines *gardhāśrita* as body-connected feeling that is not favorable to dispassion. English therefore uses 'dependent on greed' rather than 'attached to sense-pleasure.'
sbh2.0:75.46: The seven *bodhyaṅga* (awakening-factors) listed at 75.39–46 in connection with the dharmas-foundation-of-mindfulness — mindfulness, dharma-discrimination, energy, joy, tranquillity, concentration, equanimity — anticipate the dedicated treatment at 83.6–16. The root recap at 75.46 omits *prīti* (joy), but the line is explicitly continuing the seven-factor list and 83.13–83.16 confirms joy as the third insight-side factor. At 83.13 the printed/root *dharmavinayaḥ* is contextually read as *dharma-pravicayaḥ* (dharma-discrimination), the required awakening-factor, and the English marks that repair conjectural. The functional analysis there divides them three+three+one: three on the *vipaśyanā* side (dharma-discrimination, energy, joy), three on the *śamatha* side (tranquillity, concentration, equanimity), and mindfulness as belonging to both. The pattern — calm and insight as two parallel three-fold tracks with mindfulness as their pivot — is one of the chapter's most important architectural arguments.
sbh2.0:77.42: The source at 77.42 begins with visible damage (`.. yena ca karoti`). The English is intentionally fragmentary and marked `[Damaged]`; without the marker the line looks like a secure smooth continuation of the action/foundation analysis.
sbh2.0:79.110: The four *samyak-prahāṇa* (right exertions) are reanalyzed as four *prahāṇa* (abandonments) at 79.110–127: *saṃvara-prahāṇa* (restraint, antidote to arisen evil), *prahāṇa-prahāṇa* (abandonment-of-abandonment, antidote to unarisen evil), *bhāvanā-prahāṇa* (cultivation, antidote to unarisen wholesome's failure to arise), and *anurakṣaṇā-prahāṇa* (protection, antidote to arisen wholesome's loss). The pair-mapping is symmetric: each evil/wholesome × arisen/unarisen quadrant yields one *prahāṇa*. The printed/root line at 79.127 says *anutpannāḥ kuśalā dharmāḥ* ('unarisen wholesome dharmas') are protected, but the protection-abandonment paragraph is explicitly about already arisen/acquired wholesome dharmas; English supplies the internally required 'arisen' conjecturally. The summary at 79.130–131 then reduces the whole system to abandoning the dark-side object and acquiring the bright-side object, not relinquishing both dark and bright alike.
sbh2.0:80.6: In the desire-concentration explanation, *chandajātaś ca* means 'with desire arisen.' Desire is the motivating predominant factor for right contemplation of the dharmas; it is not something 'borne upon' the evil unwholesome dharmas.
sbh2.0:80.13: The printed/root *samavasthāna-samudācāra-* is not the expected pair with *anuśaya* at 80.14. The standard contrast is manifest obsession (*paryavasthāna*) versus latent tendency (*anuśaya*); the English reads the intended *paryavasthāna* and marks the line conjectural/corrupt.
sbh2.0:80.38: The line at 80.38 is visibly noisy (`te pāpakā akuśalā dharmā dharma mudā haranti`). The earlier English 'instigate [him] as a wave' had no support in the available Sanskrit. The safe contextual reading is simply that, before the concentration-headed antidotes arise, the evil unwholesome dharmas present themselves again; English marks this conjectural/corrupt.
sbh2.0:80.51: The eight *prahāṇa-saṃskāra* (formative impulses for abandonment) at 80.51–69 — desire, exertion, faith, tranquillity, mindfulness, full awareness, volition, and equanimity — are the canonical eight-fold yoga that drives the *iddhipāda* to its completion. The list pairs cleanly with the eightfold path in some readings but here functions independently as the inner mechanism of how concentration-driven cultivation actually eradicates *anuśaya* (latent tendencies). At 80.61, *saṃprajanya* is full awareness / clear comprehension, not 'knowing-eagerness'; at 80.67, *viṣaya-viparokṣa* means the object is directly present, not out of sight. The same eight reappear in Sarvāstivāda *Saṃyukta-āgama* parallels to SN 51 (the *iddhipāda* samyutta). Note the doubling at 80.70 with desire/striving/faith etc. as a recapitulation list — the text is reading the eight from two angles.
sbh2.0:80.79: The etymology of *ṛddhi-pāda* (base of psychic power) at 80.79–86 is the standard Yogācāra/Sarvāstivāda gloss: as *pāda* (foot) is what one steps with, so the *iddhipāda* is what one steps onto the supramundane path with. The supramundane dharmas are themselves the supreme *ṛddhi* (prosperity, accomplishment) — not magical powers in the popular sense but the noble path-fruits. This reading deflates the more-magical popular interpretation of *ṛddhi* and grounds the four *iddhipāda* firmly in path-attainment.
sbh2.0:81.5: The faith-faculty definition concerns trust in others' attainment — specifically the attainment of the Teacher and disciples — not the practitioner's own realization of the Teacher. *Samāpattyarthena* is read here as 'in the sense of attainment,' not as meditative equipoise.
sbh2.0:81.10: The five *indriya* (faculties) and five *bala* (powers) share the same five members — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom — and differ only in *strength*: as *indriya* they predominate over their respective domains; as *bala* they are uncrushable by their respective obstacles. The chapter's mapping at 81.27–82.4 ties each indriya/bala to a specific previously-treated schema: faith → four *avetya-prasāda* (serenities of clear knowing), energy → four *samyak-prahāṇa*, mindfulness → four *smṛtyupasthāna*, concentration → four *dhyāna*, wisdom → four *ārya-satya*. This is a deliberate architectural argument: the five-fold indriya/bala framework is *the same content* as the prior schemata, indexed by predominance.
sbh2.0:82.12: The fire-stick simile at 82.12–83.4 maps the *nirvedha-bhāgīya* sequence onto the stages of fire-kindling: rubbing-effort = five *indriya*; first warmth in the lower stick = *uṣma-gata*; warmth rising upward = *mūrdhan*; smoke = *satya-anulomikī kṣānti*; flameless fire falling = *laukikāgra-dharma*; flame born = supramundane fluxless *bodhyaṅga* dharmas. The simile is preserved in Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* VI.18, indicating shared Sarvāstivāda-Yogācāra material rather than a Yogācāra innovation. Its function: to make vivid that the *nirvedha-bhāgīya* are *signs* of supramundane fire approaching, not the fire itself.
sbh2.0:83.21: The path-aggregates analysis at 83.21–23 is the canonical *triśikṣā*-mapping of the noble eightfold path: right speech + right action + right livelihood = *śīla-skandha*; right mindfulness + right concentration = *samādhi-skandha*; right view + right intention + right effort = *prajñā-skandha* (the *prajñā-skandha* identification is implicit here but explicit at 86.47–50 where they are called *vipaśyanā*). The printed/root line at 83.21 omits right speech, but the later recap at 86.38 has the full *samyag-vāk-karmānta-ājīva* triad; the English supplies right speech conjecturally. The same three-fold partition is canonical in Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* VI.74.
sbh2.0:84.3: The right-view definition runs across 84.3, 85.1, and 86.1. It has two components: the direct realization of reality at the time of the awakening-factors, and the later delineation of that same realization by wisdom. The prior wording 'realization that has gone forth' over-read the damaged/extracted *yathāvigata* and obscured the two-part structure.
sbh2.0:86.24: The local phrase is *āpakāntāni śīlāni*, not *nirvedha-bhāgīya-śīla*. The explanation at 86.25–29 derives the label from the cluster *iṣṭa*, *kānta*, *priya*, and *manāpa*: these virtues conform to what has long been loved or esteemed by the noble ones.
sbh2.0:86.29: The bracket now follows local *āpakānta*. The English keeps 'in conformity with what is loved' because 86.25–28 glosses the object through the cluster *iṣṭa*, *kānta*, *priya*, and *manāpa*.
sbh2.0:86.44: The line defining the effort factor ends with noisy *samyagvyāyāmaśamathaḥ*. The noble eightfold path has right effort, not 'right calm'; calm is analyzed immediately afterward at 86.45–50 through right mindfulness and right concentration. English therefore marks the line conjectural/corrupt and reads the intended right-effort factor.
sbh2.0:86.55: The *darśana-mārga* / *bhāvanā-mārga* distinction at 86.53–55 is one of the chapter's most important technical pivots. The *darśana-mārga* (insight-path) abandons defilements *by mere knowledge-of-the-bound-thing* — a single insight that, once arisen, completes its work in one moment. The *bhāvanā-mārga* (cultivation-path) abandons defilements *by long-time practice* — repeated familiarization with what insight has already seen. This is why right speech/action/livelihood are placed in the cultivation-path: they require sustained living-out, not just seeing. The standard Sarvāstivāda *Abhidharmakośa* VI.28+ analysis treats *darśana* as the sixteen-moment penetration of the four truths, *bhāvanā* as everything subsequent up to arhatship.
sbh2.0:86.72: The stream-entry fruit is first tied to the abandonment of *nirvastuka* ('baseless') defilements that cause going to the lower realms. The bracket now follows local *nirvastuka-kleśa* rather than importing a normalized *apāya-gamanīya-kleśa* label. The three *saṃyojana* (fetters) — *satkāya-dṛṣṭi* (identity-view), *śīla-vrata-parāmarśa* (clinging-to-virtue-and-vow), and *vicikitsā* (doubt) — are then tied to three sociological positions at 86.74–84: the householder (whose obstacle is identity-view, which prevents engaging the path at all), the ill-stated *dharma-vinaya* (whose obstacle is virtue-and-vow-clinging, which leads to wrong practice), and the well-stated *dharma-vinaya* (whose obstacle is doubt, which prevents penetration even when training rightly). This three-way positional analysis is unusual — Pāli sources typically give the three fetters as a flat list. The functional reading here makes them a developmental sequence: each fetter is the *characteristic obstacle of its stage of religious life*, and stream-entry abandons all three at once. The English at 86.74 follows the local order (*gṛhi-pakṣa*, *durākhyāta-dharma-vinaya*, *svākhyāta-dharma-vinaya*) and renders *vicikitsātaś coccalitaḥ* as being unsettled by doubt.
sbh2.0:88.22: *Manda-rajaska* (one of slight dust) — the canonical stream-of-yogis term for the practitioner whose karmic-defilement-result coverings are minimal at the outset. The threefold *āvaraṇa* analysis at 88.24–43 is canonical: *karma-āvaraṇa* (the five ānantarya plus other intentional heavy karma), *kleśa-āvaraṇa* (intense or long defilement-states unresponsive to standard antidotes), and *vipāka-āvaraṇa* (rebirth in a realm where the path cannot arise: lower realms, certain heavens, frontier regions, or with sense-faculty impairment). The *manda-rajaska* is one in whom all three coverings are absent — the ideal recipient of the gradual training described in [sbh4.1](sbh4.1.html)+.
sbh2.0:88.39: The *vipāka-āvaraṇa* passage distinguishes two result-covering cases: birth in a realm where the noble path does not function, and birth in a realm where the path can function but this person is blocked by impairments such as deaf-mutism or hand impairment. The English should not add a negative to 88.41; the contrast depends on *apravṛtti* at 88.39 versus *pravṛtti* at 88.41.
sbh2.0:88.47: The upright-view passage is controlled by the heading *dṛṣṭiś ca ṛjvī* at 88.44 and the conclusion *dṛṣṭi-ṛjutā* at 88.63. The noisy 88.47 extraction should not be made into a separate term *dṛṣṭi-tṛpti* ('satisfaction-in-view'). The four modes are conviction/faith, guilelessness, well-considered Dharma-meaning free from doubt, and twofold-path practice that proceeds to distinction.
sbh2.0:89.2: The six *pudgala-prajñapti* (person-designations) — *śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, brahmacārin, bhikṣu, yati, pravrajita* — are reclaimed Vedic/general-religious terms whose Buddhist redefinitions paragraphs 89–93 work out. Standard procedure in the Yogācārabhūmi: take a term used outside the dispensation, distinguish its conventional usage from its noble-Dharma usage, and define the noble usage by reference to defilement-abandonment. The earlier bracket *vrātya/yati* imported a non-local label; the root and later definition at 92.2-92.13 use *yati*. The closing quotation at 89.39–44 is the canonical *cattāro śramaṇa* sūtra preserved in Pāli (DN 16, MN 11) — affirming that true śramaṇas exist only where the eightfold path is known.
sbh2.0:89.11: *Mārga-jīvin* is a path-person label: one who lives by the path, i.e. one whose practice is still alive and path-conducive. The English should never read 'liver of the path,' which looks anatomical rather than verbal.
sbh2.0:89.24: *Dharmanetrī* is guidance or leading by Dharma, not *dharma-cakṣus* ('Dharma-eye'). The path-teachers are those who hold the conventional Dharma-Vinaya and set Dharma-guidance in motion.
sbh2.0:89.26: The printed/root line *pṛthagjana-kalyāṇakā ātmahitāya pratipannā śajjinaḥ mārgadeśikāḥ* is corrupt in the transition into the *mārga-jīvin* explanation. The surrounding lines require the group of good worldlings engaged in practice for their own benefit, then explicitly conclude at 89.29 and 89.31 that these are *mārga-jīvinaḥ* ('those who live by the path'). The English marks the line conjectural and reads the internally required category.
sbh2.0:90.16: The local root has *tad-antara-prahāyī* and *tad-atyanta-prahāyī*. The brackets now follow the local forms rather than importing normalized *vimadhya-* or *ātyantika-* labels.
sbh2.0:92.11: The defilement-restraint list contains harmful and malevolent applied thoughts, then a cluster of lower-realm-producing states: covetousness, malevolence, wrong view, false view, anger, resentment, concealment, spite, and the like. The earlier 'malicious joy' was not a good rendering for *pradāśa*, and 'bad-bound matters' obscured the *āpāyika/nairayika/durgatigāmin* sequence.
sbh2.0:93.10: Damage note for 93.10–93.19: the source has several lacunae in the person-designation and time-distinction transition. The surrounding argument remains legible enough to translate, but these damaged segments should not be used for close philological claims without checking a parallel witness.
sbh2.0:93.21: *Kṣiprābhijña* in this path-typology context is 'quick-knowledge' or 'quickly knowing,' matching the painful/pleasant practice by slow/quick knowledge matrix earlier in the chapter. It should not be inflated to 'quick supernormal knowledge' here.
sbh2.0:94.6: The four *māra* — *skandha-māra* (aggregate-māra), *kleśa-māra* (defilement-māra), *maraṇa-māra* (death-māra), *devaputra-māra* (deva-son-māra) — are the canonical Yogācāra fourfold. The local root uses *maraṇa-māra*, not the normalized *mṛtyu-māra*, so the bracket follows the local form. The Pāli tradition has variations (sometimes with *abhisaṅkhāra-māra*, conditioning-māra, instead of one of these). The Yogācāra functional analysis at 94.13–15 is unusual and worth noting: the four māras are *causally interlinked* — death-māra is what one dies *from* (aggregates), and what one dies *into* (new aggregates), and what makes one yield to death (defilements that obstruct surmounting it), and what blocks the surmounter (deva-son-māra creating obstacles).
sbh2.0:96.1: The worldly-path dispassionate worldling remains under Māra's sway whether he remains here or is reborn elsewhere, because worldly dispassion does not cut the underlying bondage. At 96.22, *dṛṣṭy-anumata* is approving or agreeing with a view, here in the company of evil friends, not simply following one's own view.
sbh2.0:98.1: The fruitfulness-of-undertaking analysis at 98.1–22 turns on three causes: *indriya-paripuṣṭi* (perfecting of faculties), *anuloma-avavāda* (conforming instruction), and *samādhi* (concentration). The printed/root opening says *caturbhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ* ('by four causes'), but only three are listed and 98.21–22 explicitly says three; the English follows the internal count and marks the number conjectural. At 98.7 the root reads *kevalavān* ('alone/complete'), but the matrix requires the same strong-concentration condition as 98.11 and 98.21; the English supplies 'strong' conjecturally. The combinations are reduced in practice to the rule: fruitless if any one of the three is missing, fruitful only when all three are present. Duplication at 98.16–18 is in the source — likely a scribal repetition of the immediately-prior case (98.13–15); preserved in the translation but flagged.
sbh2.0:94.10: Restored from PDF 4797-4799. The pre-existing JSON had a stitched clause `teṣāṁ teṣāṁ niścayaprāptaḥ antarāyam upasaṁharati` that collapsed three clauses of source: the closing of the *kleśamāra* definition, the *maraṇamāra* definition, and the opening of the *devaputramāra* definition. The māra-typology now reads in source order: skandhamāra (94.8) — kleśamāra (94.9-10) — maraṇamāra (94.11) — devaputramāra (94.12 onwards).
sbh2.0:90.5: Restored from PDF 4748-4749. The pre-existing JSON had a stitched clause (visible in the doubled `tatra tatra`) that collapsed the *jātibrāhmaṇa* definition into the start of the *saṁjñābrāhmaṇa* definition, dropping the birth-lineage description (*kulajāto, yonijo, mātṛsambhūtaḥ, utpanno mātṛtaḥ pitṛtaḥ*). The three brāhmaṇa categories — by birth, by designation, by engagement — now appear in full source order.
sbh2.0:59.136: Restored from PDF 3882-3887. The pre-existing JSON had a stitched clause that collapsed the *sa-cchidra-vāhana* question (59.135) directly into a different topic — the four laukika-path attentions (ānulomika, prātipakṣika, prasadanīya, pratyavekṣaṇīya) — dropping the detailed definitions of three of the four progressive *manaskāras*: *sa-cchidra-vāhana* (interrupted), *niś-chidra-vāhana* (uninterrupted), and *anābhoga-vāhana* (effortless). With this restoration the manaskāra-taxonomy (whose listing is at 59.126) now has all four definitions in place: bala-vāhana at 59.127-134, sa-cchidra-vāhana at 59.135-138, niś-chidra-vāhana at 59.139-140, anābhoga-vāhana at 59.141-142. These four are the structural counterpart to the nine mental abidings at sbh3.1, as the cross-reference at sbh3.1:13.2 indicates.
